
=================================================================
#48 Huangdi (皇帝)  (648 March)
Arc: The Chunchu Era · place: changan · tone: imperial intrigue
Logline: Everyone on earth wants something from the Son of Heaven. Most of them bring tribute. Chunchu brings an offer.
=================================================================
[0] ── SCENE: The Son of Heaven ──
[1] ¶ Everyone on earth wants something from the Son of Heaven. Most of them bring tribute. Chunchu brings an offer.
[2] [TERM Huangdi · Emperor (皇帝): Huang, the god-kings of the dawn of the world. Di, the lord of heaven. The first man to put the two words together burned the books. Every other ruler on earth is a king. This one is the Son of Heaven, and he would like it said in that order.]
[3] ¶ The embassy comes in at the hour the street drums stop. The great avenue opens ahead of it, a hundred and fifty paces wide and perfectly empty.
[4] [MAP 648: Silla’s one harbour, one sea, and a road to Chang’an long enough to rehearse a speech forty times.]
[5] ¶ Chang’an is a hundred and eight walled wards, locked at the drums. At the lodging a ward chief is waiting with a lamp and a register. He does not look at the prince’s face. He counts heads the way a man counts sacks, and writes a number.
[6] Ward chief: Silla embassy. Eleven mouths. / Eleven in, eleven out. If one of you dies, report it to the ward before the morning drum. / We’ll send a man to make up the count.
[7] King Muyeol: Make up the count. / …With whom?
[8] Ward chief: With a man.
[9] King Muyeol: Any man?
[10] Ward chief: The register hasn’t got a column for names, sir. Only for the number.
[11] [CARD Kim Inmun: Chunchu’s second son. He reads Tang characters better than his father would like.]
[12] ¶ Inmun reads the register over the man’s shoulder. Eleven. He will live in this city for most of his life, and in every count it ever makes of him he will be one stroke in that column.
[13] ¶ The tenth stroke is a young Hwarang called Jukji, who writes down everything. The eleventh is On Gunhae, who carries his master’s coat and has not said a word since the harbour. The ward chief does not look at him either.
[14] ── SCENE: The Audience Hall ──
[15] The Second Emperor: Your name is “Spring and Autumn”…? Then is your younger brother called “Warring States”?
[16] King Muyeol: My father revered the Confucian learning, and named me after Confucius’s “Spring and Autumn Annals”.
[17] King Muyeol: Confucius said it: if the name is not correct, speech does not follow. / So I dare to ask. Your Majesty has my name. / What is the correct name for me to call Your Majesty?
[18] ¶ The hall stops breathing. Nobody in Chang’an says that name. A clerk by the door shuts his eyes, the way men do just before a horse kicks.
[19] The Second Emperor: You may call Us Majesty. Everyone under heaven does. / That name is received when We give it. Not when it is asked for.
[20] King Muyeol: Since the age of the Three Zhou, Samhan and the Central Plain have been inseparable. / And now Your Majesty has accomplished the great work of restoring the glory of Han — / are you not the Guangwu of this age?
[21] King Muyeol: Silla will accept investiture from the Great Tang. / Your Majesty has armies beyond counting; Chunchu has knowledge of Samhan. / Samhan is known best by the people of Samhan. / To accomplish a great work, must not great men gather?
[22] The Second Emperor: You would teach Us Samhan?
[23] King Muyeol: Someone taught it long before me. Sunzi: know the other, know yourself, and a hundred battles hold no danger. / At Ansi, Your Majesty knew yourself. / Your Majesty did not know who was standing on the wall.
[24] ¶ Several ministers discover something interesting on the floor. The emperor does not move for one long breath. Then he laughs, and the floor stops being interesting.
[25] The Second Emperor: Yes — there is something between us that fits.
[26] The Second Emperor: Your Divine Country sends me the most cunning man in Samhan. / Good. I have already spent a summer failing against the Eternal General. I prefer allies who can count.
[27] King Muyeol: Then count one thing for me, Majesty. When the lips are gone, the teeth are cold. / If Silla is the lip, Liaodong is the tooth.
[28] The Second Emperor: That is what a minister of Yu told his duke. / Do you know how that story ends, Spring-and-Autumn?
[29] King Muyeol: I know how it ends for the duke who didn’t listen, Majesty.
[30] ¶ Both men know the rest of that story. Neither says it out loud, which is the most honest thing either of them does all evening.
[31] ¶ After the hall, a smaller room. A go board. The emperor keeps the platform. Chunchu sits on the floor. Stones click in the dark.
[32] ¶ Chunchu opens in the far corner. Then he turns, and starts pressing the stones right beside his own.
[33] The Second Emperor: Befriend the far, strike the near. You play it the way Qin did. / Qin ate the world with it.
[34] King Muyeol: And how long did Qin keep the world, Majesty?
[35] The Second Emperor: Long enough to name it. / But on this board the far one is you. You want Us to be the far friend who strikes your neighbours. / On a go board, Spring-and-Autumn, the far friend usually takes the corner as well.
[36] King Muyeol: Then I’ll have to play the corner first, Majesty.
[37] The Second Emperor: Chunchu. It is a waste, a man like you growing old on the frontier. / Come and serve in my imperial guard. / A house in Chang’an, a title, and bring your son as well.
[38] King Muyeol: …You honour me, Your Majesty.
[39] The Second Emperor: “You honour me” means “no.”
[40] King Muyeol: Your Majesty reads people well.
[41] The Second Emperor: I read people well. It is why I am still alive. / That, and Saluzi.
[42] King Muyeol: Saluzi, Majesty? / …Forgive me. I don’t know the name.
[43] The Second Emperor: No, you would not. He never held office. / No title, no fief, no son at court for me to promote. Outside Luoyang he took an arrow in the chest that had my name on it, and brought me back to camp with it still in him. / The most loyal warrior I have ever had. Perhaps I shall introduce you, before you go.
[44] King Muyeol: …I would very much like that, Majesty.
[45] The Second Emperor: That one means “yes.” Good.
[46] The Second Emperor: Fine. Leave the son, then. Do not say “no” to that one.
[47] ¶ Inmun stays in Chang’an. He will be there, on and off, for the rest of his life.
[48] ¶ Nobody has said the word army yet. Chunchu has asked for it three ways. The emperor has answered with a house, a title and a hostage.
[49] ¶ Between audiences he asks, as idly as a foreign envoy can ask anything, after a general named Saluzi. A clerk of the Ministry of War spends an afternoon in the rolls on his behalf and comes back apologetic. There is no Saluzi: no rank, no fief, no tomb, no widow drawing a pension. Either the emperor’s most loyal warrior is dead, or he is the only man in Chang’an without paperwork. Chunchu finds he wants to meet him more than he wanted to meet the emperor.
[50] ── SCENE: The History Office ──
[51] ¶ The Ministry of War can’t find him a general, so Chunchu tries the historians. Chu Suiliang receives him among the shelves. He once refused to let the emperor read his own diary. Now he’s high enough to choose what he says, and careful enough to say very little. Everyone in Chang’an knows how this emperor got the throne: at a palace gate, over two dead brothers. Nobody in Chang’an says it.
[52] King Muyeol: Lord Chu. A small question from a small country. / His Majesty came to the throne by way of the Xuanwu Gate, I’m told. The ninth year of Wude, the sixth month, the fourth day—
[53] Chu Suiliang: Which gate?
[54] King Muyeol: …The Xuanwu Gate. The north one.
[55] Chu Suiliang: There is a gate there. A very fine gate. Nothing happened at it.
[56] King Muyeol: And the fourth day of the sixth month?
[57] Chu Suiliang: The third was a fine day, Prince. The fifth was finer. / I can recommend either.
[58] King Muyeol: I’d heard the account was rewritten.
[59] Chu Suiliang: Harmonized, Prince. / Here we say harmonized.
[60] King Muyeol: In the old state of Jin, they say, the historian Dong Hu wrote that the chief minister had killed his lord, and would not change a word. Dong Hu’s brush.
[61] Chu Suiliang: Dong Hu was a fine historian. / And that Jin is gone.
[62] King Muyeol: Then I’ll take the fifth. / I’ve always liked a fine day.
[63] ── SCENE: The Imperial Academy ──
[64] ¶ Chunchu asks one favour no envoy has asked in years. He would like to watch the rites to Confucius at the Imperial Academy, and sit in on the lectures. The clerks are so surprised that they say yes. Sons of dukes and sons of clerks sit the same examination here. A good enough answer can put any of them in a purple robe.
[65] ¶ Chunchu was born one step below the throne, by his own council’s arithmetic, and has spent his life sitting anywhere but the chair. He watches a clerk’s son recite the Odes without one slip, and does not say a word for the rest of the afternoon.
[66] Kim Inmun: …Father?
[67] King Muyeol: Study, Inmun. Here it’s faster than blood.
[68] ¶ He asks for one more thing before he goes: Tang court dress, cut to Silla measure, so that his officials at home will look like the officials in this city. The emperor is delighted, and sends a chest of it.
[69] ¶ He thanks the emperor at his desk. The talk wanders.
[70] King Muyeol: Your Majesty… forgive a barbarian’s question. / You mean… they all absolutely obey you, no matter what?
[71] The Second Emperor: If they do not, they stop being useful. / Useful men live longer. I did not invent that. I only wrote it down.
[72] King Muyeol: And if the great families were to meet, Majesty. All of them, in one room. And agree that you should no longer be emperor? / …What happens then?
[73] ¶ The emperor looks at him for a long moment, as though Chunchu had asked what happens if the sun is voted out of the sky. Then he laughs, and it is not a polite laugh.
[74] The Second Emperor: Agree? Agree to what, precisely? / There are not two suns in the sky, nor two kings over one people. Nobody takes a vote on the sun.
[75] King Muyeol: In Silla, Majesty, someone did. The Harmony Council deposed a king. He was my grandfather. / They met, they agreed, and he went home.
[76] The Second Emperor: He went home. / They told a king he was no longer king, and he… went home. He did not kill them? Not even one, to make the point?
[77] King Muyeol: …Not even one, Majesty.
[78] The Second Emperor: Then your kings are boats with no water under them. Anyone at all could tip one over.
[79] King Muyeol: Then who overturns the boat, Majesty?
[80] The Second Emperor: The water. Not the passengers. / The ruler is the boat and the people are the water. Water carries the boat, and water overturns it. / We fear the water. Your uncles are passengers.
[81] ¶ The emperor shakes his head, still smiling, and goes back to his memorials. Chunchu says nothing more. He is watching the brush in the emperor’s hand: one man, one brush, and at the far end of it a province three months away. Nobody in this palace will ever meet in a room to vote that hand off the paper. He cannot stop looking at it, the way a poor man looks at a jade he will never afford, and he does not let one particle of it reach his face.
[82] ── SCENE: The Gyuku Ground ──
[83] ¶ The days between audiences belong to someone else. The crown prince — **Li Zhi**, twenty years old and still allowed to laugh with his shoulders — steals Chunchu from the memorial-hall the way a younger brother steals an older one from a funeral, and takes him to the imperial **gyuku** ground.
[84] [CARD The Third Emperor: Li Zhi. Heir to everything, and the first man in Chang’an to laugh.]
[85] ¶ They play gyuku until the dust makes them the same colour. Li Zhi talks like a man who has waited his whole life to be ordinary with somebody dangerous. Chunchu lets him.
[86] The Third Emperor: When I am emperor — / No. That sounds like a curse. When the years have been kinder — / I will still want this. A friend who does not need my title to stand upright.
[87] King Muyeol: Then keep me as I am. / When you are emperor I will still be a man from a small country with a large grudge. / That is the only honest introduction I have.
[88] The Third Emperor: Good. / Brothers, then — of the inconvenient kind.
[89] King Muyeol: Of the inconvenient kind.
[90] ── SCENE: The Six Steeds ──
[91] ¶ That night the emperor dismisses the lamp-bearers and carries the lamp himself, down a gallery behind the Liangyi Hall that no envoy has been shown. Along the wall runs a band of six stone horses, each long panel cut in low relief from drawings by the court painter. They are meant for the mountain at Zhaoling, where they will stand guard over a tomb. Nobody has told Chunchu whose.
[92] The Second Emperor: Leave the lamp to me tonight. I have carried heavier things down darker corridors. / You have seen my clerks, Spring-and-Autumn, and my six boards, and my very tedious seal. You have not yet met the ones who actually made me emperor. / Allow me to present them.
[93] King Muyeol: …Horses, Your Majesty?
[94] ¶ He lifts the lamp to the first panel. Out of the black comes a horse in mid-stride, cut so shallow it seems to be passing through the wall rather than standing on it. The emperor lays his palm on its hoof, as if to keep it from leaving.
[95] The Second Emperor: **Baitiwu**. Black from ear to tail, and white at all four feet, as though he had walked through snow and declined to wipe them. / **Baitiwu** ran all night. Two hundred li. He woke to find me at his gate, and simply… surrendered. I have never in my life been so exhausted, nor so pleased with anyone.
[96] ¶ They walk on. The lamp swings at his side, and their two shadows climb the wall ahead of them, larger than either man, stepping over the carved hooves.
[97] ¶ At the third panel he does not stop. The lamp slides over a horse with a man standing at its chest, and the emperor walks on as though he has not seen it.
[98] The Second Emperor: Not that one. Not yet.
[99] ¶ Ten paces on, the emperor stops so abruptly that Chunchu nearly walks into his sleeve. This time he holds the lamp high over his head, and a grey horse comes out of the stone at full gallop.
[100] The Second Emperor: **Qingzhui**. Grey-dappled, and fast as a rumour. / At Hulao, a rival who called himself king came with a hundred thousand men to relieve Luoyang. I had perhaps three thousand five hundred riders, and I elected to be rude about the arithmetic. / Five arrows struck him, Chunchu. Every one of them from behind.
[101] King Muyeol: From behind… all five?
[102] The Second Emperor: All five. They could not hit him from the front. By the time they drew, he was already past them.
[103] ¶ At the sixth panel he brings the lamp close enough to warm the stone, and counts along the horse’s flank with one finger, arrow by arrow, the way a man counts the graves of his own soldiers.
[104] The Second Emperor: And **Quanmaogua**. Curly-coated, black-muzzled, quite the ugliest horse in the empire, and the most stubborn. / The last of the rebels, by the Ming River. Nine arrows: six in front, three behind. Count them, if you like; the masons were most particular. / He stood until the fighting was done. Then he lay down, as though he had only been waiting for permission.
[105] ¶ They reach the end of the gallery. Past the sixth horse the timber frame runs on, and inside it the stone is smooth.
[106] King Muyeol: And the seventh, Your Majesty? For Liaodong?
[107] The Second Emperor: There is no seventh. I rode to Liaodong on a perfectly good horse whose name I find I have mislaid.
[108] ¶ Then he turns and walks back the way they came, past the arrows, past the grey horse and the black, and Chunchu follows the lamp. He stops at the third panel, the one he would not look at, and this time he lifts the light all the way up.
[109] The Second Emperor: **Saluzi**.
[110] ¶ Chunchu hears the name before he understands it. He looks at the purple horse in the stone, and at the man carved at its chest, and back at the emperor, and an afternoon of the Ministry of War’s rolls rearranges itself in his head. Horse after horse, name after name, and not once has it occurred to him.
[111] King Muyeol: …Saluzi. / Your most loyal warrior. The one who never held office. / Majesty. He is a _horse_.
[112] The Second Emperor: The finest in the empire. I never said he was a man, Spring-and-Autumn. You supplied that yourself. / Most of my ministers make the same mistake about themselves.
[113] King Muyeol: I had a clerk of your Ministry of War search the rolls for him. / All afternoon.
[114] The Second Emperor: (laughs, and it carries all the way down the gallery) / Did you. Then somewhere in my ministry there is a clerk who believes the Silla prince is hunting my generals. I shall have to promote him.
[115] ¶ Then the laugh goes out of him the way a lamp gutters, and he looks back up at the stone.
[116] The Second Emperor: Purple, the colour of a fresh bruise, and quite as proud of himself. / Outside Luoyang I galloped too far ahead, as young men will, and found myself entirely alone with the pretender’s army, which was deciding what to do with me. An arrow took **Saluzi** in the chest. He did not fall. He stood there with it in him and waited for me to think of something. / One of my generals rode in, gave me his own horse, and drew the arrow out of mine with his bare hands while the enemy looked on. That is he, at the chest. The only man I have permitted onto these walls. / **Saluzi** carried me back to camp, and then he died. He waited until it was convenient for me. I have never quite forgiven him the courtesy.
[117] ¶ He does not move on. He sets the lamp on the floor beneath the panel, which is not a thing emperors do in front of foreign princes, and lays his hand flat on the carved neck, and leaves it there.
[118] The Second Emperor: I have had sons, Spring-and-Autumn. Wives. More ministers than I can name. / He is the only one who never once asked me for anything.
[119] ¶ Chunchu does not interrupt. It is the first time in Chang’an he has seen the emperor need an audience rather than command one.
[120] The Second Emperor: These are going to the mountain. When I am laid in Zhaoling, the six of them will stand outside the door and wait. / He shall have the place nearest. He always did insist on being out in front.
[121] King Muyeol: Then they’ll have a long wait, Majesty. And horses do so hate waiting.
[122] ¶ The emperor picks up the lamp and turns. It hangs low at his knee now, and from below his face is all hollows.
[123] The Second Emperor: I am not joking, you.
[124] ¶ He coughs into his sleeve, a small dry cough, and looks at the sleeve a moment too long before he folds it away. Chunchu has seen men do that. None of them were emperors.
[125] The Second Emperor: Chunchu. You grew up in Samhan, so—
[126] The Second Emperor: Chunchu… promise me this one thing. / Accomplish this one great work for me…! / Goryeo is the single failure of my life. / Baekje will be the single failure of yours. / I—your country—
[127] ¶ He sets the lamp down again at the foot of the purple horse.
[128] The Second Emperor: I do not go to Liaodong for land. I have mountains and rivers enough to bore a man to death. / When the two of them are settled, everything south of Pyongyang, and the whole of Baekje, is Silla’s. For your peace. Forever.
[129] King Muyeol: …May I have that in writing, Majesty?
[130] The Second Emperor: (laughs) An emperor’s word is the writing, Spring-and-Autumn. / Every clerk in this city will remember it for you.
[131] The Second Emperor: The Son of Heaven makes no jokes. You know the saying. / A boy-king of Zhou once cut a paulownia leaf into a tally and handed it to his little brother as a game. ‘With this, I enfeoff you.’ / His historian wrote it down, and the brother got a country. It was called Tang.
[132] King Muyeol: …Then I’ll trust the clerk, Majesty.
[133] ── SCENE: The Farewell Banquet ──
[134] ¶ At a banquet meant to impress the Silla guest, the Second Emperor’s laughter is the loudest thing in the hall. Behind a screen a concubine listens the way a strategist listens — counting who drinks, who flinches, which foreign prince the emperor calls brother.
[135] ¶ Halfway through, the emperor calls for brushes. In Chang’an, a banquet without verse is just dinner.
[136] The Second Emperor: Spring-and-Autumn of Silla, We give you a poem. Ministers, attend. / We wrote it for an old minister, in the years when Our brothers could not bear Us. He was the one man who could not be bought with profit or frightened with death.
[137] [POEM Given to Xiao Yu (賜蕭瑀) [The Second Emperor] (Quan Tangshi (全唐詩) bk. 1, Tang Taizong, Given to Xiao Yu (賜蕭瑀)): The gale shows which grass is strong;* the ruined age shows which minister is true.† What does a brave man know of right? The wise man keeps benevolence close.]
[138] ¶ The hall applauds, the way halls do. Then all of it turns toward the Silla guest. An answer is expected. A barbarian is expected to need until morning.
[139] The Second Emperor: Answer. And use Our rhymes.
[140] King Muyeol: Grant me the time it takes to empty one cup, Majesty.
[141] ¶ He does not empty it. He sets it down full, asks for the brush, and writes on his knees at the low table.
[142] [POEM Answering on the Emperor’s rhymes (奉和) · Chunchu’s own verse [King Muyeol]: At the sea’s corner a stubborn grass grows;* only under heavy frost does the lonely minister show. It will not lie down for a mad wind,† but its heart already leans to the Sage Lord’s benevolence.]
[143] ¶ Nobody in the hall says anything, because nobody knows yet what the emperor thinks. The emperor reads it twice. The second time, his lips move on the last line.
[144] The Second Emperor: We said the wind tests the grass. / And he takes Our grass and hands it back with Us as the wind! / “The gentleman’s virtue is the wind, the small man’s is the grass; let the wind pass over it, and the grass must bend.” He has put the Analects on Our rhymes and handed it to Us! / The mad wind is Baekje, and the place to lean is Us. We have never been asked for an army so pleasantly.
[145] The Second Emperor: Zhi — keep this one. Men who can rhyme on their knees are rarer than honest generals.
[146] ¶ Twenty characters. He has asked for an army, flattered an emperor out of his own classics, and called his neighbours a bad wind, without one word anybody could quote back at him.
[147] ¶ Behind the screen **Wu** does not merely listen. She works the room without entering it: a glance that steadies a nervous maid, a smile that slows a minister’s cup, a silence that turns every eye in the hall back to the foreign prince.
[148] [CARD Wu Zetian: Wu, a lady of the inner palace. The screen is doing very little of the hiding.]
[149] ── SCENE: The Lodging ──
[150] ¶ On the morning before he is to leave, a parcel comes to the lodging from the palace. Inside are rubbings of two steles in the emperor’s own hand, and a new history of the Jin dynasty, so fresh from the Historiography Office that the paste on the bindings is still soft.
[151] Kim Inmun: The paste is still wet, Father. / Is this one… harmonized?
[152] King Muyeol: Fresh. Here they harmonize it before the paste dries. / Read it slowly anyway. We’ll want to know what the Jin are allowed to have done.
[153] ¶ One of the two rubbings is for a temple at Jinci, raised to a little brother who was once handed a leaf. Chunchu reads the first column and laughs out loud. He asked the emperor for that promise in writing. Here it is, in the emperor’s own hand.
[154] ── SCENE: HALLWAY ──
[155] ¶ Night in a long palace corridor. Red columns, white plaster, a little light leaking from the next hall. Somewhere a banquet is still going. Out here it’s quiet enough to hear footsteps behind you.
[156] ¶ Before the embassy horses leave Chang’an, a woman from the emperor’s household asks for a moment that is not on any schedule. The clerks pretend not to see. That is how courts invent privacy.
[157] Wu Zetian: Chunchu!
[158] King Muyeol: ?
[159] ¶ He turns in the dark.
[160] Wu Zetian: Chunchu… you are the one from the country with the woman king, correct?
[161] King Muyeol: Yes, ma’am.
[162] Wu Zetian: How is she doing?
[163] King Muyeol: Well, the conservative faction initially had its doubts about whether a woman could take the throne. / However, as with all things in life, the problem turned out to be more in the mind than in reality. / She has proven to be a wise and capable king, and is well-beloved by the p—
[164] Wu Zetian: Yes, yes. But that wasn’t my question… / How is _she_ doing?
[165] King Muyeol: …Oh. / (smiling) She is doing well. She has found a lot of peace in her life. Thank you for asking.
[166] Wu Zetian: Can you deliver her a message for me? / Tell her to never stand down in the face of hardship. / In the violent and competitive world of men, tell her I want her to become a defiant woman — a woman who can look any man in the face and see an equal. A woman who can conquer worlds with her glance. / Tell her to stay silent — not in submission, but in strength. / For if there is anything I have learned in the Emperor’s Court, it is that silence is the true mark of power…! / (determined, fierce)
[167] King Muyeol: (astonished) …Oh, I see. / W-who did you say you were again?
[168] Wu Zetian: (leans over to his ear, whispers something)
[169] ¶ Whatever she says takes less than a breath. When she draws back she is still smiling — the social smile of a woman who could host a banquet or end a lineage with the same mouth.
[170] King Muyeol: (paralyzed in fear, wide-eyed, scurries away back toward Silla)
[171] Wu Zetian: (waves back flirtatiously)
[172] The Third Emperor: (calling from behind) Wu! You haven’t been scaring our guests away, have you?
[173] ── SCENE: The Last Game ──
[174] ¶ Chunchu gets as far as the next courtyard. A eunuch is waiting there with a lamp, as if someone had told him exactly how fast a frightened prince walks. The emperor is not asleep. The go board is out.
[175] The Second Emperor: Sit. One game, and then you may go.
[176] ¶ They play without talking. Chunchu takes the far corner again. This time the emperor lets him have it.
[177] The Second Emperor: Li Shimin.
[178] King Muyeol: …Sir?
[179] The Second Emperor: You asked my name, did you not. / That is my name. / Li Shimin.
[180] ¶ The room does not react, because the room does not understand what has just happened. Only two men in it do.
[181] ¶ No law forbids what he has just done; something older and more total than law forbids it. He has handed a foreign prince the one thing his own sons cannot say out loud.
[182] King Muyeol: A magnificent name. / So an emperor is a man like the rest of us. / …Though it will be a dreadful nuisance to avoid writing it.
[183] ¶ Chunchu makes the joke because he can feel the man needs to be laughed with, now, or the moment will curdle into something neither of them can carry out of the room.
[184] The Second Emperor: You told Us once: if the name is not correct, speech does not follow. / Is it correct now?
[185] King Muyeol: …Now the speech can follow, Majesty.
[186] [CARD The Second Emperor: Li Shimin, the Second Emperor of Tang. Nobody in Chang’an writes his name. He has just said it to a foreigner, on purpose.]
[187] ── SCENE: The Mingde Gate ──
[188] ¶ On the last morning Li Zhi rides down to the Mingde Gate himself, which crown princes do not do.
[189] ¶ At the gate Chunchu does not bow like a foreign guest. He bows like a man watching his younger brother try on a coat that will never come off.
[190] The Third Emperor: Spring and Autumn. / You really are going.
[191] King Muyeol: I said I would. / Inconvenient brothers keep their appointments.
[192] The Third Emperor: Then when you are king — / write to me as you wrote when we were only dust and horses. / I will need one person who remembers my name was Zhi before it was an era.
[193] King Muyeol: Yes…! / Now—— we have won this war…!
[194] ¶ Chunchu says it the way a man says a prayer he has been saving.
[195] ¶ He leaves Chang’an with the alliance sealed and his son still inside the wall. The gates do not ask who was afraid.
[196] [MAP 648: The same sea home. It has Goguryeo boats on it now.]
[197] (monologue) King Muyeol: I’ve met many powerful people in my life. Generals, kings, emperors. But there has only been one person who I’ve been afraid of. During that short conversation, that woman’s eyes paralyzed me in fear.
[198] ── SCENE: On Gunhae ──
[199] ¶ A day and a night out to sea, a second hull takes their wind. Not a war fleet. A Goguryeo patrol boat, the kind that sniffs a sea-road and reports who used it. They’ve been sniffing this one since Chunchu walked out of Yeon’s prison.
[200] [CARD On Gunhae: Chunchu’s attendant. The same height as his master, which will matter.]
[201] On Gunhae: My lord. The small boat.
[202] King Muyeol: That cap is heavy.
[203] On Gunhae: Then I will wear it.
[204] ¶ **On Gunhae** takes the high cap and the great coat — Tang’s gift, cut to be read at two li as a prince. He sits high on the deck, where the mast makes a chair of shadow, and does not wave.
[205] ¶ The patrol closes. A shout across the water names the wrong man, and is satisfied. They board. They take the coat. The annal will say they killed him. Chunchu’s small boat is already a darker strip of sea.
[206] ¶ He reaches the home shore in a boat Chang’an wouldn’t have bothered to count.
[207] ¶ Eleven went in at the drum. Inmun is still inside the wall. On Gunhae is wherever the patrol left him.
[208] King Muyeol: Nine. / …Report it to the ward before the morning drum. / He never asked me for anything either.
[209] ¶ **Chunchu has watched one brush move an empire. Now he wants that brush in Silla. The Harmony Council hasn't noticed yet…!**
